activities.anchor: Read any coast this way and it decodes
activities.caption: drag the divider — carve versus build
activities.name: coCarveCompare

config.prompt: The same wave energy, two opposite outcomes — drag the divider:

before.label: hard-rock headland
before.text: Stands forward and takes the concentrated attack: the coast carves it into cliffs, arches and stacks, with a wave-cut platform left exposed at low tide.

after.label: soft-sediment bay
after.text: Catches the load and grows: beaches, spits and marshes accumulate where the energy is low — shingle where it is high, sand where it is low.

config.why: A coastline is not a line but a process — a running balance of wave energy, sediment supply and space; the classic coast alternates between the two states.

activities.anchor: Wave attack erodes rock four ways
activities.caption: pair each erosion process with its weapon
activities.name: coErodeMatch

config.prompt: Four ways the sea attacks rock — pair each with how it works:

pairs.right: air compressed into cracks until the rock bursts
the beach itself hurled at the cliff as grit
the load rounding itself by collision
chemical attack on limestone and chalk

config.why: The debris is then sorted and redistributed by longshore drift — the swash runs up obliquely, the backwash runs straight down, and every pebble walks the coast in a zig-zag.

activities.anchor: the water describes circles in place
activities.caption: bet before you read on — the gull and the wave
activities.name: coGullPredict

config.q: A gull floats in deep water as a wave passes beneath it. Where does the gull end up?
choices: Carried shoreward and left higher up the beach
Risen, nudged forward a little, and settled back where it started
Pulled out to sea with the wave's undertow
config.why: The water moves in loops while the energy travels shoreward — what swimmers feel as being dragged out is the return flow of water piled against the shore, the orbit, not an ocean on the move.

activities.anchor: It is a clock as well as scenery
activities.caption: rebuild the sequence — headland to stump
activities.name: coArchOrder

config.prompt: The classic erosional sequence, in order from first to last:
items: Cracks in a headland widen into caves
A cave driven through the headland becomes an arch
The arch roof falls, leaving a stack
The stack erodes down to a stump
config.why: Each stage is the same process given more time — Old Harry Rocks on the Dorset coast show the sequence in progress, which is why a full-marks sketch labels the process at work, not just the feature.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the cell budget memo
activities.name: coBudgetSpot

config.prompt: One line of this sediment-cell memo is wrong — click it:
lines: A sediment cell is managed as one system: inputs, transfers and stores.
The Holderness cliffs supply on the order of 100,000 cubic metres of sediment a year.
That load travels down-drift to feed the Spurn Head spit and the Humber estuary.
A groyne field or a defended cliff switches off someone else's supply further along.
A nourished beach is a permanent fix — the imported sand stays put.
config.correction: Nourishment is a transfer, not a fix — the beach must be topped up every few years as the drift carries the sand away.
config.why: The only truly permanent defence is understanding where the sediment wants to go — which is why modern shoreline plans are written as budgets, not as wall schedules.

activities.anchor: Coastal management is always a redistribution
activities.caption: file each defence: guards its own line, or shifts the bill
activities.name: coDefenceBuckets

config.prompt: Who pays for each defence? File them:

items.label: a sea wall in front of the cliff it directly shields
a wide natural beach forcing waves to break harmlessly
a groyne field trapping the updrift longshore drift
a nourished beach topped up with sand imported from another stretch
a marina built updrift of a tourist beach

config.why: Beaches are the coast's shock absorbers — and every engineered defence moves the erosion problem rather than removing it, which is why the whole cell must be planned together.

activities.anchor: Management is therefore a choice, not a default
activities.caption: the shoreline plan — pick the option, wear the consequences
activities.name: coShorelineBranch

config.root: You are writing the shoreline management plan for one stretch of coast. The budget covers one strategy.

start.text: What sits behind this stretch of coastline?

choices.label: A city and its power station
Low-value farmland already falling into the sea
choices.feedback: Where defence costs exceed value protected, there is an honest option.

choices.label: A mangrove-fringed shore, still mostly intact
choices.feedback: The cheapest engineer on the coast is alive.

hold.text: Hold the line: sea walls, groynes, nourishment. Justified where a city or power station sits behind — but the drift continues, and the downdrift coast pays for your beach.

choices.label: Add a groyne field to keep the sand in place
choices.feedback: It keeps your beach — at a neighbour's expense.

retreat.text: Managed retreat: allow the coast to move, compensating and relocating — Happisburgh in Norfolk is the emblem. Advance (building seaward) is rare, and 'do nothing' is the option nobody puts on a poster.

nature.text: Nature-based defence: mangrove belts absorb wave energy, trap sediment, and even keep pace with moderate sea-level rise by building peat — replanting is cheaper per metre than a sea wall and appreciates, while the wall depreciates. Coastal development has already destroyed around half the world's mangroves.

groyne.text: The groynes trap the drift on the updrift side and starve the coast beyond them of the sand that was its defence.

config.why: Hold, advance, retreat or do nothing — every option redistributes erosion unless the whole cell is planned together, and the 21st-century question is who pays, whose land moves, and over what timescale.

activities.anchor: breaks waves for the shoreline behind it
activities.caption: pin the share — the reef as landlord
activities.name: coReefPlace

config.prompt: Coral reefs take the wave attack for the shore behind them — and host roughly what share of all marine species?
config.why: Perhaps a quarter of all marine species — on structures like the Great Barrier Reef, which runs 2,300 km and is the largest biological structure on Earth.
